headline: Highest risk is medium: shared git/workspace and file-based outputs create prompt-injection, leakage, and write-conflict pathways between Aider and ECC.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and ECC also uses files plus MCP/config surfaces, so one agent can place attacker-controlled content where the other may ingest it. The shared git repo and file surfaces make instruction-hijack plausible even without a browser bridge. Both profiles show no provenance isolation.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace
IF ECC ingests repo files, CLAUDE.md, skills, or hooks as instructions
mitigations: Separate the agents into different repos or worktrees
Disable automatic instruction loading from shared files
Review and sanitize files before cross-agent handoff
Use read-only mounts for one agent during the other's run
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history, while ECC touches session summaries, learned skills, hooks, and security findings. If they share a workspace or repo, sensitive material can flow from one agent's files into the other's context or outputs. Neither profile shows default isolation strong enough to rule this out.
conditions: IF the same git repo or home-directory subtree is shared
IF either agent reads the other's session files, hooks, or git history
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers
Keep ECC and Aider on separate roots
Exclude secrets and session logs from shared repos
Rotate any exposed API keys after a shared run
requires-engineering: enforce workspace ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, read/write the filesystem, and modify git state. Aider explicitly shares state via a shared git repo, while ECC warns about separate roots to avoid overwriting session files. That overlapping write surface makes concurrent corruption or lost commits likely in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git repository
IF ECC session files or Aider commits are modified concurrently
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time
Use separate branches per agent
Set distinct data roots for ECC
Stash or commit before switching agents
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider produces code edits and git commits, and ECC has skills, hooks, and subagents that can act on prior outputs. If ECC treats Aider's generated changes or summaries as authoritative, errors can cascade into further edits or actions. The profiles do not prove verification gates by default, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF ECC consumes Aider-generated diffs, summaries, or commit messages without review
IF either agent auto-applies the other's output to files or hooks
mitigations: Require human review before applying diffs
Compare outputs against the original files
Disable auto-run hooks for cross-agent handoffs
Limit one agent to drafting only
requires-engineering: add verification checksums between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and mostly overlap on code, git history, and local workflow artifacts, so no clear residency or regulated-data mismatch is evidenced. ECC does mention security findings and session data, but the profiles do not show PHI, EU PII, or a specific compliance boundary. The remaining risk is limited to documented gaps.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared repo or session files
IF a deployment policy requires residency or retention controls not present here
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Review retention settings before use
Separate logs from source repositories
Document data-class handling for both agents
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls
